newsitem.title: USA: Arafat, Netanyahu in marathon Mideast crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Arafat, Netanyahu in marathon Mideast crisis talks.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat held long talks over chicken and couscous at a Middle East crisis summit on Tuesday but there was no word of any deals despite the promising atmospherics.

On the contrary, on the only concrete point divulged by officials at the Washington summit, Israel said it stood firm against U.S. pressures to agree to a final date for a pullback of Israeli troops from the West Bank city of Hebron.

Even so, all sides were pleased that the two-day summit hosted by U.S. President Bill Clinton led quickly to impromptu marathon bargaining between Arafat and Netanyahu, and to a cordial mood for talks planned Tuesday night and Wednesday.

"I understand it was very relaxed and comprehensive with the aim of discussing all the problems that came up," an Israeli official said of the Arafat-Netanyahu talks that began at a White House luncheon and ran nearly three hours.
"It was after all the first opportunity for them to truly sit and go over all the subjects."

Israeli sources said they expected Netanyahu and Arafat to meet again later on Tuesday evening. "Its very likely. I assume that since the mood is good, progress has been made," one Israeli government source said.

Clinton called the summit in a desperate bid to prevent a collapse of the continuing Middle East peace process following renewed violence that killed 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis in the West Bank and Gaza last week.
U.S. and Israeli officials insisted they had no details on what Netanyahu and Arafat -- whom some feared might refuse to negotiate directly at all -- had discussed.

But all argued that their long private meeting with only interpreters present in a White House residence library was a promising start toward the meeting of minds needed to rescue imperilled Middle East peace prospects.

"They left in obviously what appeared to U.S. observers to be a good mood," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry. "They walked each other out through the South Portico and shook hands and left in their respective motorcades. They clearly had a cordial meeting."

Netanyahu then met with U.S Secretary of State Warren Christopher at Blair House, a U.S. VIP guest residence across from the White House. After that, Christopher conferred with Arafat at the Palestinian presidents hotel.
There were prospects such sideline meetings might go on through the night as summit diplomacy whirred into high gear.
The White House said it expected another gathering there on Wednesday before summit results were announced.

Last week's fighting was sparked by Israel's decision to open another entrance to a tourist tunnel alongside Jerusalem's Temple Mount, holy to both Moslems and Jews. But it reflected also Arab frustrations at what they consider Israel's slow pace of pursuing peace accords.

Key bones of contention included Arab demands that Israel carry out a year-old accord for a partial pullback of its troops from Hebron, that it close the offending new tunnel entrance and loosen barriers against movement of Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank outside those areas.

Israel, which wants assurances of security against Arab violence, has proposed that non-stop talks on these points begin after the Washington summit but it reportedly refused to yield on the Hebron issue when Clinton raised it.

"Definitely it was clear the American side wants ... to set a final date (on a Hebron pullback). We were saying it is impossible," said Natan Sharansky, Israel's trade minister and a member of Prime Minister Netanyahu's delegation.
Hebron is the last major city occupied by Israeli troops in the Palestinian-run West Bank.
The Arafat-Netanyahu tete-a-tete and the whirl of followup U.S.-mediated diplomacy raised hopes nonetheless that something solid would emerge from the summit.

"The nature of the conversation today was such that it was clear they could work together and begin to have the kind of dialogue that will resolve, we hope, their differences," McCurry said as the luncheon talks were proceeding.

Clinton began the summit on Tuesday morning by meeting separately with the Israeli and Palestinian leaders. Then he hosted a 45-minute Oval Office meeting among the entire group including Jordan's King Hussein, the third summit guest.
The direct Israeli-Palestinian talk came about as the offshoot of an impromptu group lunch hosted by Clinton.
After about 20 minutes, Clinton and the King left the two main protagonists alone with their roasted chicken, couscous, carrot cake and caramalized bananas.

U.S. politics intruded right at the outset of the planned two-day summit as Clinton's election rival, Bob Dole, issued a statement insisting the interests of "our friend Israel" be protected. The White House gave Dole a chilly brush-off.

The political backdrop was further underscored when Dole and Netanyahu at first agreed to meet on Tuesday afternoon. That diversion raised some eyebrows and Dole's office later postponed it until Wednesday afternoon.
